expectedText:
PREGNANT WORKERS FAIRNESS ACT ACCOMMODATION REQUEST
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

WHO THIS COVERS
This request applies if Acme, Inc. employs 15 or more people. Federal law requires accommodating a known limitation related to pregnancy, childbirth, or a related medical condition regardless of whether that limitation would separately qualify as a disability under the Americans with Disabilities Act.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "an employer, which means a person engaged in industry affecting commerce who has 15 or more employees as defined in section 2000e(b) of this title"
  — 42 U.S.C. § 2000gg(2)(B)(i) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, covered-employer definition (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000gg)
  "the term “known limitation” means physical or mental condition related to, affected by, or arising out of pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions that the employee or employee’s representative has communicated to the employer whether or not such condition meets the definition of disability specified in section 3 of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (42 U.S.C. 12102)"
  — 42 U.S.C. § 2000gg(4) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, known-limitation definition (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000gg)
  Known gap: This is a distinct federal law from the ADA, not an extension of it — a limitation doesn't have to be severe enough to count as a disability to trigger this specific accommodation duty. This document doesn't restate the ADA's own accommodation clause; the two laws overlap in some situations but aren't the same test.

THE ACCOMMODATION DUTY
Acme, Inc. must make a reasonable accommodation for Jordan Lee's known limitation unless doing so would impose an undue hardship. Acme, Inc. can't require Jordan Lee to accept a different accommodation than the one actually reached through the interactive process, can't require Jordan Lee to take leave — paid or unpaid — if another reasonable accommodation would work instead, can't deny Jordan Lee an employment opportunity because of the need to provide this accommodation, and can't take adverse action against Jordan Lee for requesting or using one.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "It shall be an unlawful employment practice for a covered entity to— (1) not make reasonable accommodations to the known limitations related to the pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions of a qualified employee, unless such covered entity can demonstrate that the accommodation would impose an undue hardship on the operation of the business of such covered entity; (2) require a qualified employee affected by pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions to accept an accommodation other than any reasonable accommodation arrived at through the interactive process referred to in section 2000gg(7) of this title; (3) deny employment opportunities to a qualified employee if such denial is based on the need of the covered entity to make reasonable accommodations to the known limitations related to the pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions of the qualified employee; (4) require a qualified employee to take leave, whether paid or unpaid, if another reasonable accommodation can be provided to the known limitations related to the pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions of the qualified employee; or (5) take adverse action in terms, conditions, or privileges of employment against a qualified employee on account of the employee requesting or using a reasonable accommodation to the known limitations related to the pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions of the employee."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 2000gg-1(1)-(5) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, accommodation duty and prohibited practices (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000gg-1)
  "the term “qualified employee” means an employee or applicant who, with or without reasonable accommodation, can perform the essential functions of the employment position, except that an employee or applicant shall be considered qualified if— (A) any inability to perform an essential function is for a temporary period; (B) the essential function could be performed in the near future; and (C) the inability to perform the essential function can be reasonably accommodated"
  — 42 U.S.C. § 2000gg(6) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, qualified-employee definition (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000gg)
  Known gap: This duty extends further than it might appear: someone temporarily unable to perform an essential job function still counts as a qualified employee entitled to this protection, if the inability is temporary, the function could be performed again in the near future, and the inability can be reasonably accommodated in the meantime. That's a real, specific carve-out this law adds — a temporary inability to do part of the job doesn't by itself remove someone from this protection.

ACCOMMODATION REQUESTED
Jordan Lee requests a reasonable accommodation related to pregnancy, childbirth, or a related medical condition.

Description of the limitation: _______________________________________________
Requested accommodation: _______________________________________________
Expected duration (if known): _______________

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to acknowledge this request.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________

—
Groundtruth v1 demo · every "Verified" citation links to a real, checked source.
